Figure 2:Overview of FRED.We interpret the usage of a VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator,i.e.,𝐡=𝐟θ​(ϵ|𝐨t,𝐜){\mathbf{h}}={\mathbf{f}}_{\theta}(\bm{\epsilon}|{\mathbf{o}}_{t},{\mathbf{c}}). From this perspective, we
enhance𝐡{\mathbf{h}}through self-distillation to predict target representations𝐡τ{\mathbf{h}}^{\tau}extracted from noisy future observations𝐨t+1τ{\mathbf{o}}_{t+1}^{\tau}by a momentum teacher, while using historical observations𝐨t−H:t{\mathbf{o}}_{t-H:t}as conditioning input to exploit richer temporal context.

Figure 3:Visualization of the training and evaluation setup.(a) For zero-shot environment generalization, we train FRED on the DROID(Khazatsky et al., 2024)dataset and evaluate it on diverse tasks in a new real-world environment without task-specific fine-tuning. (b) For human-robot co-training, we train FRED either on robot demonstrations alone or jointly on robot demonstrations and human videos, and evaluate it on both in-domain robot tasks and human-to-robot skill transfer tasks.
Figure 5:DROID evaluation setup.The setup consists of a Franka Research 3 robot arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, a wrist camera, and left and right exterior cameras.

Figure 6:DROID evaluation tasks.Task visualization for four task suites: (a) in-domain easy, (b) in-domain long-horizon, (c) out-of-domain, and (d) object grounding.Clear Tablerepeats the pick-and-place step until the table is empty.
Figure 7:OpenArm evaluation setup.It consists of the two 7-DoF OpenArm arms and a ZED 2i stereo camera mounted on the 2-DoF neck, together with the objects used in the evaluation tasks.

Figure 10:OpenArm evaluation tasks.The seven tasks, grouped into (a) in-domain atomic, (b) in-domain composite, and (c) human skill transfer. Each task is shown by the initial and final egocentric frames of one episode.
